notes: One engine-assisted reviewer compared paired and separately searched Stockfish lines before viewing classifier outputs.

cases.rationale: After Rh6+, White's rook is less able to support c6 and Black's rook checks make the connected g- and h-pawns dangerous. The better counterplay remains credible, though the searches differ on its value.
Nf4 permits Nxh5 and an attack through the knight checks, with Qxh6+ in the paired line. Qxd2+ removes this material and king attack by exchanging queens.
Rc5 leaves the advanced e-pawn alive and allows Black to activate bishop and rook with repeated checks. Rxe3 removes it before White reorganises the rook and king.
Kc7 makes Nb5+ answerable by taking c6. After Kb8, Rb4+ drives the king away and the white rook maintains the pass-pawn pressure.
Both branches lose the same a-pawn. The independent replies give equal evaluations, with no separate error attributable to Kh2.

After Bf8, both searches show a7 and a8=Q surviving Black's sequence of checks. The compared Kg7 lines give Black tactical activity before the pawn can convert, while lasting restraint remains unclear.
Re7 coordinates against d7 while Black's king can shift to f8. Rf8 leaves White's rooks to reposition with the same advanced pawn and reduces Black's activity.
The rook exchange following d8=Q frees Black's a-pawn to promote and exchange itself for White's rook. After Be7, both lines show Rxa2 removing the same pawn before promotion.
g3 allows d2 with tempo and the forced Rxd2 Bxd2 Qxd2 liquidation. The alternative can take the original d3 pawn before that advance and keep both rooks.
The two viable lines change the rook exchange and White's checking opportunities. Both still favour Black and the choice does not yield a specific promotion consequence.
Both bishop and king choices retain the drawn ending in the paired and reply searches.
Rf3+ is the leading choice and both searches let White take the b3 pawn.
Bxe4 and Nxd6 maintain essentially equivalent evaluations and both resolve the d6-pawn.
Qf6 is the leading choice, with the king taking e6 after White's checks in both analyses.
Kxh3 is the leading choice. The later exchange on e4 takes place after the pawn has been removed.
Rxd3 is the leading choice and removes the opponent's advanced pawn before White develops.
Kg6 and Rxa6 have equivalent evaluations. The independent continuations show similar drawing prospects and removal of the a6 pawn.
Rxb6 is the leading choice and removes the pawn. Subsequent central play does not identify a distinct mistake.
Qxf7 removes the pawn in the leading branch and the independent reply. The subsequent rook attack does not establish an inferior decision.
Rxa6 is the leading choice. The capture and recapture resolve the pawn without a measured mistake.
